articles.title: A New CVE Was Published. Do You Know Which of Your Applications Are Affected?
articles.excerpt: A New CVE Was Published. Do You Know Which of Your Applications Are Affected? Imagine that a security advisory announces a vulnerability in a widely used software library. Your team maintains several…
articles.body: A New CVE Was Published. Do You Know Which of Your Applications Are Affected? Imagine that a security advisory announces a vulnerability in a widely used software library. Your team maintains several applications, multiple container images and a collection of internal services. Some projects use the affected library directly. Others may include it through nested dependencies. The first question is not how quickly you can patch the library. It is much simpler: Where exactly are you using it? If your organization does not maintain an accurate inventory of software components, answering that question can take hours or even days. This is one of the problems Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is designed to solve.
articles.author: Marek „Netbe” Lampart

articles.title: My search box scored 1.00 on a query it understood nothing about
articles.excerpt: On 21 November someone typed 18米高8米宽 into the search box on my site. That means "18 m high, 8 m wide" — a question about scaffolding, arriving from a comment thread about a job site. The search return…
articles.body: On 21 November someone typed 18米高8米宽 into the search box on my site. That means "18 m high, 8 m wide" — a question about scaffolding, arriving from a comment thread about a job site. The search returned a table of rebar hook lengths and a chart of bricks per cubic metre of masonry. Both results were served at a relevance score of 1.00 . The query contains no noun. Not one. It is two dimensions and nothing else, and my matcher looked at it and said: perfect match, here you go. This is about the arithmetic that made that inevitable, why the obvious fixes don't help, and the four-line gate that replaced a scoring problem with a refusal to guess. The failure has two stages, and the first one behaved correctly Search on the site is a plain substring AND over an index string per card.

articles.title: The Cell, Not the Team: Three Roles That Make One Engineer Accountable
articles.excerpt: Part 1 ended with a unit of delivery the size of one person. This is the part where that person stops being a heroic exception and becomes a safe default. Part 1 argued that the atomic unit of deliver…
articles.body: Part 1 ended with a unit of delivery the size of one person. This is the part where that person stops being a heroic exception and becomes a safe default. Part 1 argued that the atomic unit of delivery has moved. When synthesis becomes nearly free, the scarce input is no longer the person-hour that writes the change but the judgment that decides whether it should exist. A structure whose every interface is priced by headcount cannot absorb a resource priced at zero, so the bottleneck moved downstream into verification and the org chart stayed where it was. That leaves an uncomfortable question, and it is not a motivational one. If the unit of delivery is now a single engineer carrying end-to-end responsibility, what has to be true for that to be safe ? Not faster. Safe.

articles.body: TL;DR NVIDIA Dynamo v1.6.2 (tagged 2026-11-05) is a patch release on v1.6.1, and the two changes worth your attention are small in code and large in operations. First, a TensorRT-LLM prompt longer than the engine's max_num_tokens now returns HTTP 400 invalid_request_error instead of HTTP 500 api_error , and the worker keeps running. Second, SGLang decode and aggregated workers get an opt-in --freeze-gc-after-init flag ( DYN_SGL_FREEZE_GC_AFTER_INIT ) meant to reduce streaming stalls in long-running workers. Backend versions are unchanged from v1.6.1: SGLang v0.5.21, TensorRT-LLM v1.3.0rc29, vLLM v0.31.0. Below, the release notes' statements are kept separate from my own arithmetic, and the charts are marked illustrative. Why does a 500 versus a 400 change your serving load?

articles.title: robots.txt can't block AI crawlers, but something can
articles.excerpt: Your robots.txt file does not block anyone. It is a text file full of polite requests, and the standard behind it says so in plain words. RFC 9309, the IETF specification for the Robots Exclusion Prot…
articles.body: Your robots.txt file does not block anyone. It is a text file full of polite requests, and the standard behind it says so in plain words. RFC 9309, the IETF specification for the Robots Exclusion Protocol, states that the rules "are not a form of access authorization." That matters more than it used to. Your site is now read by AI crawlers that collect training data, search bots that decide whether you appear in chatbot answers, and fetchers that pull your pages when a user asks a question. If you want a say in any of that, it helps to know what robots.txt actually does, who is listening, and what to add when a request is not enough. robots.txt is a convention, not a control RFC 9309 formalized the Robots Exclusion Protocol in 2022.

articles.title: A tempo slider that's off by default: half time, double time and a 90 BPM starting point
articles.excerpt: I build FightNome, so this post is about my own app. FightNome is a pad-work trainer for boxing, Muay Thai, kickboxing and MMA. A recorded human voice calls strikes on the beat of a backing track, and…
articles.body: I build FightNome, so this post is about my own app. FightNome is a pad-work trainer for boxing, Muay Thai, kickboxing and MMA. A recorded human voice calls strikes on the beat of a backing track, and you throw them on a bag, on pads or in the air while the phone sits in your pocket. Because everything happens on a beat, tempo is the main thing that decides how hard a round feels. You'd expect a big tempo slider on the first screen. There isn't one. What the app does instead Workouts run at 90 BPM by default. The settings screen says so in one line, calling 90 BPM a pace built for clean technique. If you want to change it for a whole workout, you turn on "Tempo control" in Settings and a workout-wide slider appears. The range it can cover is 74 to 128 BPM.

articles.title: SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper stage ever caught by 'chopsticks,' Elon Musk says
articles.excerpt: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. Rather, it will go on display as a museum piece, according to company founder and CEO Elon Musk.
articles.body: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship 's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX 's Starbase site in South Texas. Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk , who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen. "In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit .

articles.excerpt: The BepiColombo spacecraft will finally arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet.
articles.body: Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth. The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency ( JAXA ) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet. The big moment will come after an orbit-insertion burn, which is scheduled to begin today at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT) and last for 37 minutes. BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio.

articles.body: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com , a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed. A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com. The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 20, 1998:  Russia launches 1st module of International Space Station as construction begins on the largest human-built structure in orbit
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 20, 1998, the first piece of the International Space Station launched into orbit. It was just one piece, but the foundation of something much larger.
articles.body: On Nov. 20, 1998, the first piece of the International Space Station launched into orbit. The 42,000-pound module is called Zarya, and it's about the size of a tour bus. Zarya launched on board a Russian Proton rocket . Two weeks later, NASA's STS-88 shuttle mission aboard Endeavour brought the Unity module into space. The STS-88 astronauts connected the two modules in orbit. Zarya was built by the Russians, but it was paid for by the United States. NASA contracted a Russian company to build it for half the price of what the American company Lockheed Martin would have charged. These days, Zarya is mainly used for storage and for external fuel tanks. The module also has docking ports for Russian Progress cargo ships and Soyuz spacecraft that carry crews to and from the space station.
